item.title: Sen. Rob Sampson to lead smallest GOP caucus in CT history
item.dc:creator: Andrew Brown
item.description: State Sen. Rob Sampson of Wolcott will lead the GOP Senate caucus of just three members, including Sens. Eric Berthel and Henri Martin.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Rob Sampson was selected this week as the next Republican minority leader in the Connecticut Senate, setting him up to lead the smallest caucus in the chamber’s history with just three members.

Sampson, a Wolcott resident who has served in the legislature since 2011, was already one of the most recognizable Republicans in the General Assembly because of his frequent appearances on the Senate floor, where he has filibustered many of the Democratic leaders’ bills in recent years.

In his newly elected leadership position, Sampson will become one of the most prominent figures in the Connecticut Republican Party, which is seeking to rebuild after devastating electoral losses across the state during this year’s midterm elections.

Sampson, by default, will become the highest-ranking Republican office holder in the state, given the party doesn’t hold any statewide constitutional offices and hasn’t held a seat in the state’s congressional delegation since 2008.

This week, Sampson and Sen. Eric Berthel, who was chosen as the Senate’s No. 2 Republican, issued a statement about their ascendence to the leadership posts, which were left empty after eight Republican-held seats were lost Nov. 3.

In the press release this week, the two Republican lawmakers vowed to rebuild their party’s numbers in the General Assembly, which have steadily declined since President Donald Trump’s first term, and they took a passing shot at some of the outgoing members of their own party.

The statement referred to “Republicans in positions of authority who were satisfied simply to remain in the minority.” And it accused those unnamed individuals of setting aside Republican principles when it was convenient.

That stands in contrast to what Sampson is known for in the upper chamber: regularly speaking for hours on legislation he opposes.

[RELATED: Which Senators talked the most during CT’s legislative session?]

In an interview on Tuesday, Sampson said he did not want to frame the incoming Senate Republican caucus as the opposition party, and he suggested he was willing to work with his Democratic colleagues on bills he agrees with.

But he said he intended to use what little power the caucus maintains to highlight what makes Republicans different from the Democratic supermajority.

“If there is a failure among the Connecticut Republican Party as far as the legislature goes, it’s our inability to give a clear contrast and choice to voters,” Sampson said.

Sen. Bob Duff, who was just elected as the Senate’s new president, said the three Republicans who remain in the Senate were duly elected by their constituents, and he respects the authority that those voters entrusted to those senators.

But Duff, who represents Norwalk and part of Darien, also emphasized that Democrats now hold a 30-seat advantage in the Senate, and he said he and his Democratic colleagues intend to use those numbers to advance their agenda, which includes addressing the high cost of living in Connecticut and challenging the policies of President Donald Trump.

He said it is up to the Republicans to decide how much of that agenda they want to support.

The trio of Republicans who remain in the Senate — Sampson, Berthel and Sen. Henri Martin — received votes from roughly 65,000 people across their three districts, which cover parts of Southington, Bristol, Watertown and 19 other municipalities in the Naugatuck Valley region.

Sampson said he believes it is their job to represent every voter in the state who cast a ballot for a Republican this year. “We still represent 40% of the people across Connecticut who voted for Republicans,” he said.

Still, the senator recognized the physical and mathematical limitations to what Republicans can hope to accomplish over the next two years, considering they face a 33-3 disadvantage in the Senate.

Engaging in extended debate, Sampson said, will be more difficult in 2027 with only three Republicans available to hold the floor.

“That’s diminished to the point where I don’t know it will be effective at all,” he said. “Even if we are putting in every last bit of effort, it will be so grueling and demanding that I don’t know how long we could keep it up for.”

The lopsided makeup of the Senate, Sampson said, will also make it next to impossible for the three Republican senators to participate in all of the legislative committees.

Sampson said his small caucus is going to have to rely on their Republican colleagues in the House, who also suffered losses this year, to keep them informed about what bills are working their way through those committees.

Given all of those constraints, Sampson said, the most effective tool that he and his Republican colleagues may have are Connecticut residents. And he said Republicans need to harness that power by organizing protests at the State Capitol.

During Gov. Ned Lamont’s first term, Republicans helped to organize protests, which contributed to lawmakers dropping a proposal to implement tolls on Connecticut highways. And in recent sessions, Republicans helped to rally large groups of parents who were opposed to Democratic proposals to increase regulations over homeschooling in the state.

“I think the No. 1 thing that we will utilize as a small three-person Senate Republican caucus is the public,” Sampson said. “We’re going to work very hard to make sure that when there are bills that are onerous to the benefit of Connecticut, we are going to invest our time and energy to make sure the public is engaged.”

Sampson is also banking on the Democrats encountering divisions within their own caucus over what policies to prioritize and which direction to take the party.

“I think trying to wrangle a very large caucus of members in both chambers is just as difficult as trying to figure out what to do when you have very few,” Sampson said. “Because they’re going to run the gamut. There is going to be a wide spectrum of Democrats, from people who are pretty darn moderate to people that I would consider extreme.”

item.title: Matt Ritter won’t seek UConn presidency; to remain House speaker
item.dc:creator: Keith M. Phaneuf
item.description: House Speaker Matt Ritter said he will remain in his legislative post and hinted that Radenka Maric will continue as UConn's president.
item.content:encoded:
House Speaker Matt Ritter announced Wednesday he will remain in his legislative leadership post for a fourth term.

And the speaker, who had been weighing a stint as the University of Connecticut’s interim president, strongly hinted that UConn President Radenka Maric’s contract with the state’s flagship university would be extended beyond next June.

“My understanding is there won’t be a vacancy, so there’s nothing to consider,” Ritter told The Connecticut Mirror Wednesday evening.

The Hartford Democrat, who has held the top post in the state House of Representatives for the past six years, is expected to be reelected unanimously as speaker for another two years when the regular 2027 session convenes Jan. 6. Democrats captured 116 out of 151 seats in the chamber during last week’s elections.

“There’s a bit of relief, because I really wanted a fourth term,” Ritter said, adding that “I love UConn and really wish everybody all the best over there.”

The speaker confirmed in late October that he was considering taking UConn’s interim presidency if the post became vacant next year. Maric’s contract expires next June 30, and The Hartford Courant reported last week that she was a finalist to become chancellor of the University of Wisconsin’s main campus in Madison and was under consideration for posts at two other universities.

A UConn spokesman confirmed Wednesday only that Maric remains UConn’s president but did not discuss any possible moves.

Any extension of Maric’s contract at UConn would have to be approved by its Board of Trustees. But Gov. Ned Lamont controls most appointments to that group, and any top leadership decision would be made in consultation with his office.

“The governor has had a great relationship with President Maric, who has accomplished a lot for the university,” Lamont’s communications director, Cathryn Vaulman, said Wednesday.

And though she did not discuss Maric’s future, Vaulman added that “the governor trusts the Board of Trustees to make a decision in the best interest of the university as they fulfill their duties.”

Meanwhile, Ritter said he looks forward to tackling the many important issues awaiting Connecticut’s next legislature.

Lawmakers and Lamont are expected to overhaul the system of budget caps that have dominated state finances over the past decade. These controls have helped officials eliminate $11 billion in pension debt. But many legislators say it is time for Connecticut to invest more in affordable childcare, health, education and property tax relief.

“I’m excited for the opportunity to lead the largest House Democratic Caucus in a generation,” Ritter said. “It remains my dream job.”

CT Mirror reporter Theo Peck-Suzuki contributed to this story.

item.title: Roxbury couple moves ahead with plan to allow hikers on their property
item.dc:creator: P.R. Lockhart
item.description: Charles and Eli Copley say the town failed to explain how making their property available to dogs and walkers would violate zoning rules.
item.content:encoded:
A Roxbury couple who had threatened legal action over the town’s refusal to let them open their property to hikers and dog walkers will reopen their land later this week after town officials did not promptly respond to their requests for a clear explanation of how they were violating local zoning ordinances.

Charles and Eli Copley had previously opened part of their 50-acre property for some recreational activity, listing the property online for dog walkers and hikers interested in using their trails for a small hourly fee. The couple said having walkers on the property helps with forest management, as more walking activity would help maintain the trails and reduce invasive vegetation. 

But the town disagreed, arguing in 2025 that the couple was operating a home business, and that their specific use constituted a “dog park” in violation of local zoning rules. 

[RELATED: A Roxbury couple welcomed hikers, for a fee. The town said, ‘No.’]

When pressed by the couple, the town did not provide additional information, and also did not offer a path for relief. That eventually led the Copleys to secure representation from the Institute for Justice, a libertarian public interest law firm. 

Local zoning officials never responded to an August letter submitted to town on the couple’s behalf. When the couple tried to appeal the only response they did receive — a letter from Roxbury First Selectman Patrick Roy that defended the prohibition — the town’s Zoning Board of Appeals argued the letter didn’t constitute a zoning decision and therefore could not be appealed. 

Because the town’s zoning commission still hasn’t explained its stance, the couple’s legal representation said they’ll resume allowing people to use their trails, arguing they have a constitutional right to determine how to use their property. 

“Absent a receipt of a zoning determination expressing that the Copleys’ proposed use was impermissible, the Copleys would resume allowing low impact, private hiking and dog walking on their property,” the Copley’s lawyers wrote in a Nov. 10 letter. “The Town’s position is that, to date, no zoning officials have responded to the Copleys’ letter.”

The property will be relisted online this Friday, Nov. 13.  

In a statement Tuesday, the Institute for Justice said the couple had gone through the necessary steps to resolve the matter with the town. 

“For more than a year, the Copleys have been reaching out to local officials to get a clear answer on whether they can resume having hikers on their trails, but the town has refused to give a clear answer, so the Copleys will reopen their trails,” said attorney John Korevec. “What the Copleys want to do with their property is perfectly legitimate and any ban on allowing them to have hikers on their trails would be unconstitutional. If the town takes any action against the Copleys, we’re prepared to resume legal action.”  

A call to the Institute for Justice was not immediately returned in time for publication. Representatives for the town were not immediately available to offer comment. 

Officials argued against the Copleys, but never explained why

The saga over the walking trails dates back more than a year. After buying the Roxbury property in 2022 with plans to live in an old cottage on the land, the Copleys discovered that it needed significant work, especially when it came to the surrounding trails. 

A forester helped them learn how walking in particular would help, as it would help establish a clear trail system and limit invasive vegetation from growing around the site. In 2024, the couple listed the property on Sniffspot, an online platform that lets one “rent” out a property to dog owners. The couple also charged an hourly $10 fee, an amount that they said was largely to keep people from failing to show up for their reservations. 

Months after the listing went up, the town countered that the Copleys could not use their property in this way. But Roxbury officials never explained why, eventually prompting the couple to lawyer up. 

According to their lawyers, the town still has not responded beyond its argument that Roy’s defense of the prohibition did not constitute an official zoning decision. The only argument it ever gave was that the property was a home business and “dog park.” The couple’s lawyers said because the business occurs outside the home it cannot be counted as a home business, adding that there is no clear prohibition that should stop the couple from making the property available for walkers. 

The couple’s lawyers also argued that even if the town produced a clear argument for the ban, it would not stand up in court. 

“The town has been unable to explain how allowing people to walk outside on private property could possibly be problematic, and that’s because there is no reason,” Korevec said earlier this year. “The Copleys have done this before without incident, and to our knowledge, there’s been no complaints. ”

“Zoning codes are supposed to prevent genuine nuisances, not punish peaceful people who are doing nothing wrong,” he added. “That’s zoning abuse.”

In the Tuesday statement, Charles Copley said he hopes the matter is finally resolved.

“We’re looking forward to welcoming hikers back on our trails and we expect that the town will allow us to resume this harmless activity without any issues,” he said. “We’ve tried to be cooperative throughout this process, but it remains unclear what else we should do in order to get our trails re-opened.”
